items.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024
items.q: I was reading an article, an interview of Vince Mendoza and he was talking about two or three minutes of music

ctx.x: Yeah. You’ll take that. You had “compelling circles.” Before we get off this composing topic, I’ve seen that you’ve written some larger works, a concerto. Have you had that experience where you work — we get used to, in the jazz world, you know a song can be seven minutes long because it includes improvisation by the band members. I’m wondering, ‘cause this has happened to me, like I labor on something that’s more of a classical nature and I like it and then I play it back and I go wow, okay I have forty seconds…

It really is. Two minutes worth of music — I was reading an article, an interview of Vince Mendoza and he was talking about two or three minutes of music and how much that actually is, without any improvising. That’s a lot of music to compose to fit — yeah ‘cause we’re so used to just having something, you know just a little blues head and then the solos could take up most of the space. But yeah, it’s a challenge obviously. And I’m a huge fan of Mahler. So his time scale is huge. You know half an hour movements…
You and Alan Broadbent. He is a Mahler aficionado I would say.
